Your phone just agreed on a secret with a stranger, while the whole internet listened.
Impossible? It's called Diffie-Hellman, published in 1976.
Here it is with paint. You and a stranger publicly pick the same yellow.
Each of you secretly adds your own color, then you swap the mixed buckets in plain sight.
Add your secret color to the bucket you got, and you both end up with the exact same brown.
A spy saw both buckets, but nobody can un-mix paint. Mixing is easy. Unmixing is hard.
Computers use numbers. A power, then a remainder, is fast to compute. Reversing it is brutal.
With primes about two thousand bits long, no known classical computer can undo it in practical time.
Diffie and Hellman won the 2015 Turing Award. Your browser still uses a version of it today.
